extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys, agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether references (patents, publications, drawings, applications, electronic material, later factual references, tax-strategy limitations, etc.) qualify as prior art and what portions of those references can be relied upon in rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101/102/103 and related statutes. Contains examiner procedures, illustrative case law, and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility need not be disclosed in reference
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to constitute anticipatory prior art, a reference must identically disclose the claimed compound, but no utility need be disclosed by the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference that teaches the claimed compound and a process of making it can anticipate even if it does not disclose a use or efficacy (In re Schoenwald; Impax Labs. Inc. v. Aventis Pharm. Inc.). 'Proof of efficacy is not required for a prior art reference to be enabling for purposes of anticipation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents are relevant as prior art for all they contain
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of patents as references is not limited to what the patentees describe as their own inventions or to the problems with which they are concerned; patents are relevant for all they contain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference may be relied upon for all that it would have reasonably suggested to one having ordinary skill in the art, including nonpreferred embodiments (In re Heck; Merck & Co. v. Biocraft Laboratories). Even disclosures teaching away or showing a solution is 'inferior' do not necessarily avoid anticipation or obviousness if the reference still discloses the claimed subject matter (Celeritas Technologies; In re Gurley). See MPEP § 2131.05 and § 2145 for teaching-away discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonpreferred and alternative embodiments constitute prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosed examples and preferred embodiments do not constitute a teaching away from a broader disclosure; alternative and nonpreferred embodiments disclosed in a reference can be relied on as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclosure of more than one alternative does not teach away from any of the alternatives because it does not criticize or discourage any of them (In re Susi; In re Fulton). Even if a reference describes an alternative as 'inferior', the mere identification of alternatives does not negate anticipation or obviousness (In re Gurley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Later factual references can be used for certain universal facts
rubrics_metrics.description: In some circumstances, factual references need not antedate the filing date to be cited to show universal facts (characteristics/properties of a material, scientific truism) that are relevant to rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later publications can be cited to show evidence such as that undue experimentation would have been required (In re Corneil), that a parameter was or was not critical (In re Rainer), that a specification statement was inaccurate (In re Marzocchi), that an invention was inoperative or lacked utility (In re Langer), or that a claim was indefinite (In re Glass). However, later references impermissibly cannot be used to determine enablement or written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (In re Koller). Such references may also be used to show level of ordinary skill (Ex parte Erlich).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax strategies deemed within the prior art (AIA §14 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of novelty and nonobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103, any strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deferring tax liability ('tax strategy') is deemed to be within the prior art and cannot differentiate a claimed invention from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should: (1) construe claims per MPEP § 2111; (2) analyze 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112; (3) identify limitations relating to a tax strategy (noting exclusions); (4) evaluate claims under 102/103 treating tax-strategy limitations as within the prior art. Exclusions: (a) parts used solely for preparing tax returns or filing (software/apparatus/etc. solely for preparing filings); (b) severable parts used solely for financial management to the extent they don't limit use of a tax strategy. Form paragraph 7.06 may indicate claim limitations interpreted as tax strategy. Computer-implemented inventions remain patentable if the software/method is novel and non-obvious, but a prior art method does not become patentable merely by implementing a novel tax strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings can be used as prior art if they show all claimed structural features
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings and pictures can anticipate claims if they clearly show the structure which is claimed; the picture must show all claimed structural features and how they are put together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Origin of drawing is immaterial; drawings in design patents or utility patents can anticipate or make obvious claims. Features unintended or unexplained in the specification may still be relied upon if reasonably disclosed to one of ordinary skill (In re Mraz; In re Aslanian; Jockmus v. Leviton). Proportions in drawings not to scale are not evidence of actual proportions if the reference does not disclose scale (Hockerson-Halberstadt; In re Wright). Evaluate drawings for what they reasonably disclose and suggest.

rubrics_metrics.name: A document's label 'patent' alone does not make it available as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: What a foreign country designates as a 'patent' may not be a patent for rejection purposes under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or pre-AIA 102(a)/(b); substance of rights conferred and accessibility control availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the substance of rights and how information is controlled (In re Ekenstam). See MPEP § 2135.01 for when a document can be applied as a 'patent' in a rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret patents are not available as printed-publication prior art until publicly available (but may be used under pre-AIA 102(d) as of grant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents that are secret (insufficiently accessible to the public) are not available as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or pre-AIA 102(a)/(b) until made public, but may be usable under pre-AIA 102(d) as of their grant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A document must be minimally available to the public (laid open for inspection or disseminated in printed form) to constitute prior art (In re Carlson). The date it becomes available is the date it can be used as a 102(a)/(b) reference. A secrecy period after grant may not affect pre-AIA 102(d) applicability (In re Kathawala). See MPEP § 2128 for printed-publication issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date a foreign patent is effective as a reference is usually the award/grant date
rubrics_metrics.description: The date a patent is available as a reference is generally the date the patent rights are formally awarded to the applicant (i.e., when the sovereign formally bestows patent rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception when the patent is secret as of award date (In re Monks; In re Ekenstam). See MPEP § 901.05 for tabular dates of patenting and Chisum references for case lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of a patent-reference's disclosure when used as a 'patent' (not a 'publication')
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent document is applied as a patent (rather than as a publication), the examiner may rely on any information in the specification germane to the claimed subject matter, not just what is in the patent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclaimed details in the specification may be relied upon even if the patent is secret (Ex parte Ovist; In re Kathawala). The phrase 'invention ... patented' in pre-AIA 102 subsections has been interpreted to include all disclosed aspects of the invention. In re Fuge is not inconsistent—at least the claim scope embraces everything in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandoned applications constitute prior art only when publicly disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: An abandoned patent application may be prior art only when it has been appropriately disclosed to the public (e.g., referenced in another patent, publication, or voluntary disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An abandoned application becomes prior art as of the date the public gains access (37 CFR 1.14). Subject matter of an abandoned application referred to in a patent or published application may be relied on in a 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or pre-AIA 102(e) rejection if actually included or incorporated by reference in the patent. See In re Lund where canceled or non-carried-over subject matter was held not available. See MPEP §§ 901.02, 2136.02, 2136.03, 2154 for dates of priority and prior-art use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laid-open (published) foreign applications may be 'published' depending on accessibility and what was published
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign applications that have been laid open for public inspection may constitute 'published' documents; however, matter canceled before publication or matter not actually published may not be relied upon in certain rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 102(a)(2) or pre-AIA 102(e) rejection cannot rely on matter canceled from the application and thus not published in the issued patent (Ex parte Stalego; In re Lund). A 102(a)(1) or pre-AIA 102(b) rejection over a published application may rely on information canceled prior to publication if that information was publicly accessible at the relevant date (Bruckelmyer v. Ground Heaters). Accessibility and how the document was made available (microfilm, diazo copies, official journal announcements) control whether it is a 'printed publication' (In re Wyer).

rubrics_metrics.name: A reference is a 'printed publication' if accessible to the public (In re Wyer standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is proven to be a 'printed publication' upon satisfactory showing that the document has been disseminated or otherwise made available to the extent that persons interested and ordinarily skilled in the art, exercising reasonable diligence, can locate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The traditional dichotomy 'printed' vs 'publication' gives way to 'probability of dissemination' and 'public accessibility' in view of modern reproduction and retrieval technologies. Courts consider factors like dissemination, indexing, distribution, and accessibility (In re Wyer; I.C.E. Corp. v. Armco Steel Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic publications qualify as printed publications if publicly accessible to persons of skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic publications (online databases, internet posts, forums, digital video, social media) are considered 'printed publications' under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) and pre-AIA 102(a)/(b) provided they were accessible to persons concerned with the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internet/newsgroup posts directed to those of ordinary skill and sufficiently disseminated can be prior art (Suffolk Tech v. AOL and Google). Office policy requires recordation of search fields/results and retention of office copies for electronic documents that may not be retrievable later. Date of availability is the public posting date; absent a date, examiners may ask Scientific and Technical Information Center to find earliest publication date. If electronic abstracts differ appreciably from printed versions, each may need independent citation. See Amazon.com v. Barnesandnoble.com; In re Epstein; MPEP §§ 904.02(c), 707.05, 901.06(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of availability for internet/online disclosures is date of public posting; absence of date limits reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art disclosures on the Internet or an online database are publicly available as of the date the item was publicly posted; absent evidence of posting date (publication/retrieval date), the item cannot be relied upon as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or pre-AIA 102(a)/(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no clear posting date exists, the examiner cannot rely on the internet item as a 102(a)(1) reference but may use it to show state of the art. Examiners can request assistance to establish earliest date of publication/posting (MPEP § 901.06(a), subsection IV.G). Keep office copies of electronic documents for recordation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner need not prove actual access to a publication if it was publicly accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary to prove that anyone actually looked at a publication when that publication was accessible to the public through a library or patent office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the item was accessible to the public (e.g., library shelving, patent office availability), that suffices for it to be a printed publication (In re Wyer; In re Hall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of public accessibility required (theses and shelving/cataloging tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: A doctoral thesis placed in a university library may be prior art if indexed and shelved such that interested persons exercising reasonable diligence could locate it; mere technical accessibility without meaningful dissemination may not suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Hall: cataloging and shelving practices supported prior-publication finding for a thesis. In re Cronyn: theses shelved without meaningful indexing were not accessible. Courts examine cataloging/indexing, probability of wide circulation, and whether interested persons could locate the item. Historical Board decisions treating single-shelved copies as 'printed publication' have been criticized; determine 'probability of dissemination' and whether the work was made sufficiently accessible to the relevant public.
